title: Why beach sand burns your feet but the sea stays cool
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why is sand so hot but the sea is cold?
Why is the sea warmest in late summer?

explain.say: On a sunny day, the same sunshine falls on the beach and the sea, yet the sand gets scorching while the water stays cool. They need different amounts of energy to warm up.

draw.text: Why beach sand burns your feet but the sea stays cool

explain.say: Warming one gram of water by one degree takes about 4.2 joules. Sand needs only about 0.8, roughly five times less, so the same sunshine heats it far more.
Sand also keeps its heat in a thin top layer, while sunlight sinks deep into the clear, moving sea. At night the sand cools fast, but the sea stays mild.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Water stores far more heat per degree

explain.say: This amount of energy per gram per degree is called specific heat capacity. Water's is one of the highest of any common substance, which is why the sea is warmest in late summer.

faq.a: It is the energy needed to warm 1 gram of a substance by 1 degree Celsius. Water needs about 4.2 joules, much more than sand, rock or metal.

faq.q: Why does sand get hotter than the sea?
faq.a: Sand needs about five times less energy to warm up than water, and it keeps the heat in a thin top layer. The sea spreads sunlight deep and mixes it around, and some water evaporates and cools it.
asks: Why is sand hotter than water?

faq.q: Why is the sea warmest in late summer?
faq.a: Water takes a long time to warm up and to cool down, so the sea keeps soaking up heat all summer and reaches its warmest weeks after the hottest days.

faq.q: Why do coastal places have milder weather?
faq.a: The sea warms and cools slowly, so it keeps nearby land cooler in summer and warmer in winter than places far inland.

faq.q: Why are hot water bottles filled with water?
faq.a: Water stores a lot of heat for each degree, so a bottle of hot water gives out warmth for a long time as it slowly cools.
asks: Why use water in a hot water bottle?

facts: Water needs about 4.2 joules to warm 1 gram by 1 degree Celsius, about five times as much as dry sand.
Because water warms slowly, the sea around Britain is usually warmest in late August or September.
